citation: Makransky, G., Mayer, R. E., Veitch, N., Hood, M., Christensen, K. B., & Gadegaard, H. (2019). Equivalence of using a desktop virtual reality science simulation at home and in class. PLoS ONE, 14(4), e0214944. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0214944
discipline: educational psychology / science education (empirical, between-subjects experiment)
thesis: Tests whether Clark's methods-not-media 'equivalence hypothesis,' extended from instructional medium to physical learning context, holds when the same desktop-VR microbiology simulation is completed unsupervised at home versus supervised in a classroom; finds no significant home/classroom differences on learning outcome, intrinsic motivation, or self-efficacy, robust to prior-knowledge and goal-orientation covariates (one interaction exception on self-efficacy), and proposes felt presence — not physical location — as the theoretical mediator of this equivalence.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Frames the growth of outsourced/online virtual lab simulations (e.g., Labster, ASU/Google Daydream) replacing in-person labs; cites two prior mixed-fidelity comparisons (Reece & Butler 2017; Miller et al. 2018) as suggestive but methodologically limited; states the study's objective as testing whether high-fidelity computer-based science simulation outcomes are equivalent across home vs. classroom delivery.

sections.title: What is the equivalence hypothesis? / educational importance
sections.summary: States the equivalence hypothesis as an extension of Clark's (1983) methods-not-media theory to physical context: learning is primed by the instructional method (the simulation), not by home vs. school location. Frames practical stakes via time-on-task/engaged-learning-time and accessibility arguments for off-loading lab activities from the classroom.

sections.title: Prior knowledge and goal orientation as moderators
sections.summary: Poses two further questions: does equivalence hold across levels of prior knowledge (expertise-reversal-effect literature, Kalyuga) and across three PALS achievement-goal orientations (mastery, performance-approach, performance-avoid; Pintrich 2000)? Framed as covariates/interaction tests, not separate row-axis constructs.

sections.title: Materials and methods
sections.summary: Between-subjects design; N=112 University of Glasgow biology students (home n=62, classroom n=50), randomly assigned to complete the Labster 'Bacterial Isolation' desktop-VR simulation (~1 hour; dialoguing/controlling/manipulating/searching/navigating interactivity types, pedagogical-agent guided) either independently at home or supervised in a computer lab. Pre-test: prior knowledge (7 items, alpha .82) + PALS goal-orientation scales. Post-test: 16-item Rasch-validated learning outcome test (retention+transfer), 5-item intrinsic motivation scale (Deci & Ryan), 8-item self-efficacy scale (MSLQ). Analysis: Cohen's d with 95% CI + Bayesian 95% HDI, then ANCOVA with covariates and interaction tests.

sections.title: Results
sections.summary: No significant home/classroom differences on learning outcome (d=0.14), intrinsic motivation (d=0.02), or self-efficacy (d=0.09); robust after covarying prior knowledge and all three goal-orientation variables, except a significant interaction (p=.0263) in which mastery orientation predicted self-efficacy more strongly in the classroom group.

sections.title: Discussion — empirical, practical, and theoretical contributions
sections.summary: Concludes equivalence held across learning, motivation, and self-efficacy regardless of prior knowledge or goal orientation, extending Clark's methods-not-media view to physical context. Proposes that a well-designed VR simulation induces sufficient felt presence (citing Lee 2004) that the virtual context itself becomes the primary learning context, rendering physical location comparatively unimportant — presence framed as the theoretical mediator, not measured in this study.

sections.title: Limitations and future directions
sections.summary: Notes non-random consent (112/289 = 38.75% of eligible students), possible self-selection toward more motivated/mastery-oriented students, and that adequate pedagogical-agent guidance may be a boundary condition on the equivalence hypothesis. Calls for research on minimal prior-knowledge thresholds and how classroom follow-up should be structured.

readings.claim: The equivalence hypothesis extends Clark's methods-not-media theory to physical context: learning depends on the instructional method (the simulation) as primer of cognitive activity, not on the medium/setting (home vs. school) delivering it.
No significant home/classroom difference on learning outcome (d=0.14, 95% CI -0.24 to 0.53).
No significant home/classroom difference on intrinsic motivation (d=0.02) or self-efficacy (d=0.09).

Null differences on all three outcomes are robust to ANCOVA adjustment for prior knowledge and the three goal-orientation covariates, with one exception: a significant mastery-orientation x setting interaction on self-efficacy.

A well-designed VR simulation can induce felt presence strong enough that the virtual context becomes the primary learning context, making physical location comparatively unimportant — presence is proposed as the mediator, not measured here.

Only 112 of 289 eligible students (38.75%) consented, raising possible self-selection toward more motivated/mastery-oriented participants; adequate pedagogical-agent guidance is proposed as a likely boundary condition on the equivalence hypothesis.

tensions.axis: context-equivalence (this study's home/classroom finding) vs. context-matters (social constructivist views of learning; Part III's own VID-stratum findings)
tensions.note: The authors explicitly contrast their methods-not-media-derived finding with 'more social constructivist theoretical perspectives of learning that consider the context in which learning occurs as central to learning itself,' noting their own use of 'context' is narrower — physical location only, medium held constant.

tensions.axis: presence as theorized mediator vs. presence as measured construct
tensions.note: Presence is invoked to explain the equivalence finding but is not operationalized or measured anywhere in this study — a gap the authors themselves do not close, flagged as P/anticipatory-application when this unit is cited for a presence claim.

notes: PRIMARY SOURCE for debate axis 8 (deployment context matters vs. context-equivalence). This study's own manipulation (home vs. classroom, medium held constant) lands on the context-equivalence pole; Part III's VID-stratum findings (F1/F4/F6, vle-01-deployment-survey) land on the deployment-context-matters pole for a structurally different manipulation (presence vs. absence of the 3D layer, not location). The two are non-contradictory because they vary different variables — that non-contradiction is itself the analytically useful bridge point (P/anticipatory-application).
